notes: Expedited Commercial Court trial on shipbuilding option exercise; Langley J's construction analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Haugland v RMK Marine: simultaneous payment as condition of shipbuilding option
key_facts: Haugland Tankers held an option to buy a second oil product tanker identical to Hull No. 63 from Turkish builder RMK Marine.
The claimant served a valid declaration notice on 2 December 2004 but did not pay the 1% commitment fee required by clause 4 of the Option Agreement at the same time.
The builder sought to escape the option after currency movements made the fixed-price contract commercially unattractive and relied on non-payment after the deadline.
The parties agreed the governing issues were whether simultaneous payment was a condition precedent to valid exercise and, alternatively, whether time for payment was of the essence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited Commercial Court trial on 2 March 2005 of declaratory issues as to valid exercise of a shipbuilding option.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the claimant was not entitled to declarations that the option had been validly exercised or that the builder was obliged to enter the option contract.
enrichment.ratio: In a unilateral shipbuilding option agreement, simultaneous payment of the commitment fee with service of the declaration notice is a condition precedent to valid exercise of the option, following authorities on exact compliance with option terms.
legal_issues: Whether simultaneous in clause 4 meant payment with the declaration notice or with contract effectiveness
Whether payment of the commitment fee was a condition precedent to valid exercise
Whether failure to pay simultaneously was a promissory condition entitling termination
Construction of unilateral option contracts and acceptance in exact compliance

notes: Interim privacy injunction on ex parte application; Bell J's section 12(3) analysis is concise and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Jagger v Darling: interim restraint of CCTV footage publication
key_facts: Elizabeth Jagger sought interim relief after sexual activity with her boyfriend at Kabaret nightclub was recorded on CCTV and reported in the News of the World.
Copyright in the recording had been assigned to her by the club owner; she also relied on misuse of private information under Article 8.
The application targeted club manager John Darling and unidentified persons who supplied the footage to the newspaper.
Relief was sought only against publication of the recording or copies, not against written accounts of the incident.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim ex parte application in the Chancery Division for injunctions, preservation orders and a witness statement from the first defendant.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted restraining further disclosure or publication of the CCTV recording or copies, with preservation and witness statement orders.
enrichment.ratio: On an interim application under section 12(3) of the Human Rights Act, the claimant is likely to establish at trial that publication of covert CCTV footage should not be allowed where she had a legitimate expectation of privacy and there is no legitimate public interest in further dissemination.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant was likely to succeed on copyright and privacy claims
Application of section 12(3) Human Rights Act to restrain publication before trial
Balance between Article 8 privacy and Article 10 freedom of expression
Scope of relief where only image publication rather than written report is challenged

notes: Leading judgment on specimen counts after Canavan; CCRC reference and Tovey appeal considered together.

enrichment.short_title: Tovey and Smith: specimen counts and sentencing after Canavan

statutes_considered.title: Domestic Violence, Crimes and Victims Act 2004

key_facts: Peter Smith was sentenced on a sample indecent assault count as reflecting repeated abuse of a child over years; the CCRC referred the case because the judge may have acted inconsistently with Canavan.
David Tovey was sentenced for explosives and firearms offences plus two sample counts of racially aggravated criminal damage said to represent seventeen similar graffiti incidents.
The court reaffirmed that a defendant may be sentenced only for offences proved or admitted, not for uncharged specimen conduct.
Smith's five-year sentence on the sample count was reduced to three years concurrent; Tovey's overall eleven-year sentence was upheld.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined appeals on sentencing after trial, including a CCRC reference on specimen-count sentencing and renewed leave in Tovey's case.
enrichment.outcome: Smith's sentence on count 2 reduced from five to three years concurrent; Tovey's appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Following R v Canavan, a sentencing judge may not treat convicted counts as specimens of wider uncharged offending; the proper remedy is careful indictment drafting, continuous-offence charging where appropriate, or admitted wider conduct.
legal_issues: Whether sentencing on specimen counts for uncharged similar offences is lawful after Canavan
How prosecutors should frame indictments to reflect totality of multiple offending
Use of continuous-offence and Barton v DPP principles in magistrates' and Crown Court cases
Whether context can justify a substantial sentence on two individual criminal damage counts
linked_authorities: R v Canavan [1998] 1 Cr App R 70
R v Clark [1996] 2 Cr App R (S) 351

confidence.notes: Comprehensive appellate guidance with explicit outcomes in both appeals.

notes: Second appeal on abuse of process and lifting CPR Part 51 stay in childhood sexual abuse claim.

enrichment.short_title: B v B: second civil proceedings and stay after childhood abuse claim
key_facts: Ms B alleged repeated sexual abuse by her father between 1990 and 1996; criminal proceedings ended with partial acquittal and abandoned retrial.
She issued proceedings in 1997 mainly for a non-molestation injunction with damages added as then required, then issued fresh limitation proceedings in May 2003.
District Judge Bird struck out the 2003 claim as abusive and refused to lift the automatic CPR Part 51 stay on the 1997 action.
New evidence showed the 1997 file note that absent notice of intent to proceed by February 1998 the damages claim would be treated as withdrawn.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from strike-out and refusal to lift stay in overlapping county court claims for childhood sexual abuse damages.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; 2003 proceedings may continue and earlier strike-out and refusal to lift stay were set aside, with costs to the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Where earlier proceedings were brought primarily for injunctive relief and reasonably understood to have been withdrawn, fresh proceedings within limitation are not necessarily an abuse; overriding objective favours resolving undetermined claims rather than leaving them unresolved.
legal_issues: Whether second proceedings for the same cause of action were an abuse of process
Whether the CPR Part 51 stay should be lifted under CPR Part 3.9
Effect of an unrecorded or disputed 1997 order treating the claim as withdrawn
Application of Buckland v Palmer and Overseas Commercial Developments v Cox
linked_authorities: Overseas and Commercial Developments v Cox [2002] EWCA Civ 635

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural history, appellate order, and reasoning on both abuse and stay are clearly recorded.

notes: Major Exxon Valdez excess-of-loss reinsurance appeal; lengthy judgment on GCE sections I and IIIB.

enrichment.short_title: King v Brandywine: Exxon Valdez pollution costs and reinsurance cover
key_facts: Exxon incurred massive clean-up and liability costs after the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in Prince William Sound, Alaska.
Underwriters settled Section I and Section III claims under Exxon's Global Corporate Excess policy for hundreds of millions of dollars.
Reinsureds sought recovery from excess-of-loss reinsurers including Brandywine on the basis of those settlements.
Colman J held the reinsurers not liable where primary cover for pollution clean-up costs was absent and reinsurance lacked full follow-the-settlements protection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Commercial Court trial judgment on coverage under Exxon's GCE policy and related excess-of-loss reinsurance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Sections I and IIIB did not cover pollution clean-up costs under English or New York law and ESC had no recoverable Section I claim.
enrichment.ratio: Pollution clean-up costs were not covered by the property and general liability sections of the GCE on their true construction under English and New York law, so settlements did not create reinsurance liability where cover was absent and follow-the-settlements protection was limited.
legal_issues: Whether Section I property cover extended to pollution clean-up as removal of debris
Effect of Notwithstanding clauses excluding cover where Sections IIIA or IIIB applied
Whether Section IIIB covered Exxon's third-party pollution liabilities
Construction of seepage, pollution and contamination exclusions in retrocession policies
linked_authorities: Commercial Union plc v NRG Victory Reinsurance Ltd [1998] 1 Lloyd's Rep 80
King v Brandywine Reinsurance Co (NRG Victory) [2004] EWHC 1764 (Comm)

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but summary conclusions and appeal disposition are explicit.

notes: Out-of-time section 49 Solicitors Act appeal after strike-off; Maurice Kay LJ refused extension.

enrichment.short_title: Elliott v Law Society: refusal of late Solicitors Act appeal
key_facts: Mr Elliott, an Australian-qualified solicitor, was struck off by the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal after withdrawing from a ten-day hearing when an adjournment was refused.
The Tribunal found numerous conduct-unbefitting allegations relating to an investment scheme, many involving dishonesty, proved in his absence.
He pursued a Rule 25 rehearing and judicial review instead of a section 49 appeal within the 14-day limit in 2002.
He issued a statutory appeal in June 2004, more than two years late, after Leveson J dismissed his judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary hearing on whether an out-of-time section 49 Solicitors Act appeal should be entertained.
enrichment.outcome: Extension of time refused and appeal dismissed forthwith; summary costs of about £23,000 ordered against the appellant.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor who voluntarily withdraws from disciplinary proceedings and chooses rehearing and judicial review routes rather than a timely section 49 appeal cannot later obtain an extension of time to re-litigate the same grievance years after the short appeal period has expired.
legal_issues: Whether CPR Part 3.9 permitted extension of time for a section 49 appeal
Construction of Rule 25 Solicitors Disciplinary Proceedings Rules after voluntary withdrawal
Whether inadequate legal advice constituted good reason for delay
Interests of justice in expeditious disposal of solicitor discipline cases

notes: Attorney General's unduly lenient sentence reference; Tuckey LJ increased total sentence to seven years.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref No 150 of 2004: unduly lenient sentence for familial sexual abuse
key_facts: Lawrence Bowe was convicted after trial of indecent assaults on two stepdaughters between 1977 and 1982 and a step-granddaughter in 2003.
Offences included attempted rape of one stepdaughter and actual bodily harm after punching another when she threatened to tell her mother.
The trial judge sentenced him to a total of four years, citing age, good character and very considerable delay.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient given multiple victims, breach of trust, violence and attempted rape.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference for leave to refer a Crown Court sentence as unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; total sentence increased from four to seven years, with attempted rape increased to five years and consecutive sentences on the later victim adjusted.
enrichment.ratio: In serious familial sexual abuse involving multiple young victims, breach of trust, violence and attempted rape, a total sentence of four years after trial was unduly lenient and required substantial increase, subject to double jeopardy reduction.
legal_issues: Whether the four-year total sentence was unduly lenient
Weight to be given to offender age and stale offences
Appropriate starting point for attempted rape in intra-familial abuse
Application of Millberry and Attorney General's Reference guidance
linked_authorities: Attorney General's References of 2003 [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 499
Attorney General's Reference No 3 of 1995 [1996] 1 Cr App R (S) 26

confidence.notes: Facts, reference reasoning and substituted sentences are set out at length.

notes: School admissions mid-year judicial review; Tucker J held no material change of circumstances.

enrichment.short_title: R (A) v West Hatch High School: mid-year admissions review
key_facts: The claimant sought mid-year admission of her daughter S to West Hatch High School where two older siblings already attended after successful appeals.
An earlier year 7 application and appeal had been refused on oversubscription and efficiency grounds despite medical evidence about eczema and asthma.
The school refused to reconsider the second mid-year application, relying on paragraph 4.83 of the School Admissions Appeals Code.
S remained out of school though an alternative place seven miles away with transport was offered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a school's refusal to reconsider a mid-year admission application after siblings were admitted.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no significant and material change of circumstances and conditional costs order in favour of the school not to be enforced without leave.
enrichment.ratio: Admission of siblings after an unsuccessful appeal does not of itself constitute a significant and material change of circumstances justifying a fresh mid-year decision under paragraph 4.83 of the Admissions Code where the medical and family circumstances are unchanged.
legal_issues: Meaning of significant and material change of circumstances under paragraph 4.83
Whether sibling admission created an irrational refusal to reconsider
Lawfulness of applying siblings criteria only at initial year 7 admission
Whether fresh doctor and social worker letters required reconsideration

notes: Neighbouring land rights of way appeal; proprietary estoppel and Rule 258 overriding interests upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Sommer v Sweet: vehicular rights of way and proprietary estoppel
key_facts: Neighbours disputed vehicular access over Old Forge Yard in Monmouthshire to Forge Meadow and the Northern Field.
The Sweets claimed express, necessity and proprietary estoppel rights; Ms Sommer challenged validity of grants and registration entries.
Hart J found overriding interests under Land Registration Rules 1925 rule 258 and ordered rectification of registered titles.
A Part 36 offer beaten on judgment led to indemnity costs from June 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a four-day High Court trial granting declarations, rectification, injunctions and damages on rights of way.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; proprietary estoppel and rule 258 overriding interests upheld and indemnity costs order maintained.
enrichment.ratio: A vehicular right openly exercised and reputed to appertain to land may be an overriding interest under rule 258 binding a successor in title, and an equity arising from proprietary estoppel is not an overreachable equitable interest under section 2 of the Law of Property Act 1925.
legal_issues: Whether proprietary estoppel bound Ms Sommer as purchaser
Application of rule 258 to rights openly exercised over registered land
Whether equitable rights of way were overreached on sale
Rectification of the register and indemnity costs after a beaten Part 36 offer
linked_authorities: Celsteel Ltd v Alton House Ltd [1985] 1 WLR 204
E.R. Ives Investment Ltd v High [1967] 2 QB 379
Bakewell Management Ltd v Brandwood [2004] 2 AC 519

notes: Commercial Court appeal on D&O reinsurance claims control clause; Longmore LJ dismissed appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Dornoch v RSA: claims control clause and D&O reinsurance notice
key_facts: US class actions alleged Coca-Cola and directors made false statements causing investors to buy shares at inflated prices.
RSA reinsured part of Coca-Cola's directors and officers liability cover under a claims-made Master Subscription Policy.
Retrocessional syndicates relied on a standard Claims Control Clause requiring notice by cable within 72 hours of knowledge of loss.
RSA knew of the US complaints by mid-December 2000 but notified retrocessionaires on 19 January 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court declarations on construction of a reinsurance Claims Control Clause in D&O retrocession.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; RSA had no knowledge of actual loss before 19 January 2001 and the 72-hour condition precedent did not clearly exempt retrocessionaires from liability.
enrichment.ratio: In a liability reinsurance Claims Control Clause, loss means actual rather than alleged loss, and a party cannot be treated as knowing a loss exists while it remains unascertained and disputed; exemption clauses must be construed strictly.
legal_issues: Whether loss in the Claims Control Clause meant actual or alleged loss
Whose loss triggered the 72-hour notice obligation
Whether RSA had knowledge of loss before 19 January 2001
Strict construction of condition precedent exemption clauses in reinsurance
linked_authorities: Post Office v Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd [1967] 2 QB 363
Bradley v Eagle Star Insurance Co Ltd [1989] AC 957
Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
